title: Charlotte Perkins Gilman, The Yellow Wallpaper recast
author: Vellum
note: Confined for her own good, she learns the wallpaper until the crawl is the only way out—calm, not thriller. After Gilman, The Yellow Wallpaper, 1892.

scenes.title: The wallpaper
scenes.reentry: John said the country would fix me.

breaths.text: John said the country would fix me. He said it the way doctors say things when they have already decided: gently, and without room for reply. The house was a Victorian rental with good reviews and a locked gate. Our baby stayed in the city with my sister. Air, rest, no screens—John's protocol. He took my phone the first night and put it in the kitchen drawer "so I wouldn't spiral." In the mornings he checked that the drawer was still locked with a small padlock he had bought for luggage.

I was given the front bedroom because it had the best light. The wallpaper was the color of old mustard and bruised cream, a pattern that looked, at first glance, like vines trying to become handwriting. John laughed when I asked to strip it. "You're tired," he said. "It's just paper." He opened the window an inch and called that enough air.

At first I slept. Then I didn't. The nights were long and the radiator made a soft knocking, as if someone polite were asking to come in. I walked the room in bare feet and counted the repeats in the design. There were places where the pattern did not match—seams that lied. In those lies I began to see a second figure: a woman, or the suggestion of one, stooped behind the lattice as if the wallpaper were a fence.

John came upstate on weekends. He brought fruit and checked my notes. I was supposed to write only cheerful observations. When I wrote about the pattern he frowned and closed the notebook. "Rumination," he said. "We're past that." He kissed my forehead and slept deeply beside me while I watched the wall breathe in the dark. Once I touched his shoulder to wake him and he murmured, without opening his eyes, that I should try lavender.

By the third week the figure was clearer. She crawled when the light shifted. Sometimes there were many of her, a soft crowd moving behind the design, pressing outward. I stopped telling John. He had begun to speak about extending the rest. He said my sister was managing fine. He said the baby was thriving without my "anxious energy." On the video calls I was allowed twice a week, my sister held the baby just out of frame.

I peeled a corner of the paper one afternoon while he was at a conference call downstairs. The paste smelled sweet and chemical. Underneath was older paper, greener, also patterned. I laughed once, sharply, and put my hand over my mouth.

The woman behind the wall wanted out. I understood that without deciding to understand it. At night I whispered to her. In the morning I smoothed my hair and told John I felt stronger. He was pleased. He left early for the city and promised to return Friday. He left a printed schedule on the fridge: meals, naps, no correspondence.

Alone, I worked carefully. I tore where the seams were weakest. Dust fell into my hair. My nails split. The room filled with the dry smell of plaster. Sometimes I slept on the floor near the longest tear, cheek against the cool baseboard, listening for the soft drag of her body. Rain tapped the window like fingernails.

On Thursday I found a strip already loosened near the window, as if she had begun from her side. I pulled until my arms shook. Behind the paper the plaster was scored with old marks—nail holes, a child's height chart from some other family.

Friday evening John's headlights swept the driveway. I heard his key, his call from the stairs. I had locked the bedroom door from the inside. The wallpaper hung in long sheets around me like shed skin. I was circling the room on all fours, shoulder brushing the remaining strips, because that was how she moved, and I had learned her gait perfectly.
"I can't," I answered, and found that I was smiling. "She's out. I'm helping her stay out."

He forced the lock. He stood in the doorway with his suitcase and his careful face, and for a moment he looked afraid of me in a way that felt almost like respect. I kept crawling. The torn paper whispered under my knees. Outside, somewhere beyond the locked gate, a train passed and left the house quieter than before.

"I've got out at last," I told him, quite calmly, "in spite of you." There was only the pattern, and the place where it ended, and the soft raw wall that finally, finally, did not try to hold anyone in.
